subChunks.title: How Indexes Work — Inside the B-Tree
subChunks.hookHtml: A query that runs in 5 ms on 1,000 rows can take 5 seconds on 1,000,000 — and 5 minutes on 100,000,000. The query is the same. The difference is whether the engine can look up the matching rows or has to scan them all. Indexes are the data structure that turns scans into lookups. To use them well, you need to know what's actually inside one.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
The problem indexes solve

Imagine the apprentices table has a million rows. You run:

SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE name = 'Eleanor';

Without an index on name, the engine has no choice but to read every row and check whether name = 'Eleanor'. This is a full table scan — a million comparisons, plus the I/O cost of reading every disk page. With an index, the engine finds Eleanor in roughly twenty operations.

What's inside a B-tree index

The default index in every major database is a B-tree (technically a B+tree in most engines). It is a balanced tree of sorted keys. "Balanced" is the magic word: every leaf is the same depth from the root. That depth is approximately log_n N, where N is the number of indexed rows and n is the branching factor (typically a few hundred). For one million rows, depth is about 3. For one billion rows, depth is about 5. A lookup never costs more than a small handful of node reads.

Three properties make B-trees ideal for storage:

  • Sorted order at every level. Equality lookups, range scans, and ORDER BY can all walk the tree.
  • High branching factor. Each node holds many keys (sized to fit a disk page, often 8 KB), so the tree stays shallow even with billions of rows.
  • Self-balancing on writes. INSERT, UPDATE, and DELETE rebalance the tree automatically. The cost is paid on every write touching an indexed column.

Each leaf node holds (key, row pointer) pairs. The pointer (called a tuple identifier in PostgreSQL or a row ID in others) tells the engine where on disk the actual row lives. That is — crucially — a second place from the index itself.

The heap vs the index

The actual row data lives in the heap — an unordered file where rows are appended in insertion order. The index is a separate structure on disk pointing into the heap. The engine consults the index, finds the row pointer, then jumps to the heap to fetch the row. Two seeks, but two cheap seeks instead of one giant scan.

-- Conceptual layout:
-- HEAP (unordered):                INDEX (sorted B-tree):
--   page 4: row id=42 ...            'Adelaide' -> (page 9, slot 2)
--   page 9: row id=11 ...            'Eleanor'  -> (page 4, slot 0)
--   page 9: row id=42 ...            'Marcus'   -> (page 9, slot 1)
--   ...                              ...

Clustered vs non-clustered — engines differ

EngineDefault storage model
PostgreSQLHeap is unordered. All indexes are non-clustered (separate from the heap). The primary key is just another B-tree pointing into the heap. CLUSTER is a one-shot operation, not maintained.
MySQL InnoDBThe primary key is the table — rows are stored inside the PK B-tree's leaves. Secondary indexes hold the PK value, not a row pointer, then perform a second PK lookup to find the row.
SQL ServerTables can have a clustered index (which defines the on-disk row order) plus non-clustered indexes. Without a clustered index, the table is a heap.
SQLiteLike InnoDB by default — primary key clusters the storage. Use WITHOUT ROWID tables to make this explicit.

Most working SQL questions are dialect-agnostic, but "why is my secondary lookup in MySQL slower than I expected?" is exactly this — InnoDB's secondary index walks one B-tree to get the PK, then a second B-tree (the clustered storage) to get the row. PostgreSQL's pattern (one B-tree, then a heap fetch) is more uniform.

Hash indexes vs B-trees

Some engines also support hash indexes. A hash index maps hash(key) → row pointer. Equality lookups are O(1) instead of O(log n) — slightly faster on huge tables. But:

  • Hash indexes cannot serve range queries. WHERE xp BETWEEN 1000 AND 2000 is useless against a hash index — hashes destroy ordering.
  • They cannot serve ORDER BY or prefix LIKE 'El%' for the same reason.
  • They handle hash collisions, which complicates the implementation.

The result: B-tree is the universal default because it serves every common access pattern adequately. Hash indexes are a niche optimisation for equality-only workloads. PostgreSQL has them; MySQL InnoDB has an internal "adaptive hash" but no user-facing hash index type.

Partial indexes — only what matters

If 95% of your events table has archived = TRUE, indexing the whole column wastes space and write cycles. PostgreSQL supports partial indexes:

CREATE INDEX idx_events_active_user
  ON events (user_id)
  WHERE archived = FALSE;

The index now contains only the 5% of rows where archived = FALSE. It's smaller, faster to scan, and cheaper to maintain. Queries that include the same predicate WHERE archived = FALSE AND user_id = ? can use it. SQL Server has "filtered indexes" — same idea, different name. MySQL has no equivalent as of this writing.

The cost of indexes

Indexes are not free. Three costs to weigh:

  1. Write amplification. Every INSERT, UPDATE, or DELETE that touches an indexed column also updates the index B-tree. A table with 8 indexes pays roughly 8× the write cost for a column-touching update versus an unindexed table.
  2. Disk space. Indexes on wide columns (long strings, multiple columns) can rival the table's size.
  3. Planner overhead. The optimiser must consider every index when planning a query. Hundreds of indexes per table can slow planning enough to notice.

Practical rule: index columns you filter on (WHERE), join on (ON), or sort by (ORDER BY) often enough that the read savings outweigh the write tax. Don't index columns you only project (SELECT) or rarely query.

storyBeats.text: Cipher leads you to a smaller side-room — narrow, lit by a single lantern, lined floor to ceiling with thin index cards. Each card holds a name and a number. He plucks one out at random and lays it on the desk.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: These are the lookup cards. Every name in the apprentices ledger has a card here, and the cards are kept in sorted order. When the Headmaster asks 'where is Eleanor's row?', I do not flip through every page of the ledger. I open the card box at 'E', find Eleanor's card, and the card tells me which page of the ledger holds her row. Twenty cards consulted instead of a thousand pages. This is what an index is.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The structure inside the index is a B-tree — a balanced tree of sorted keys. Every leaf is the same depth from the root. For a million rows, that depth is about three. For a billion, about five. The cost of any single lookup is bounded — log-shaped, not linear. This is why a query on an indexed column does not get slower as the table grows. It is the single most important data-structure result in database engineering.

storyBeats.speaker: Heap and index, side by side
storyBeats.text:
-- The HEAP holds the rows in insertion order:
-- page 4 slot 0:  (id=42, name='Eleanor', xp=2400, ...)
-- page 9 slot 1:  (id=11, name='Marcus',  xp=1200, ...)
-- page 9 slot 2:  (id=88, name='Adelaide', xp=900, ...)

-- The INDEX on (name) holds sorted keys + pointers into the heap:
-- 'Adelaide' -> (page 9, slot 2)
-- 'Eleanor'  -> (page 4, slot 0)
-- 'Marcus'   -> (page 9, slot 1)

-- A WHERE name='Eleanor' query:
-- 1. Walk the B-tree on name: ~3 hops to find 'Eleanor'
-- 2. Follow the pointer to (page 4, slot 0) in the heap
-- 3. Return the row

-- Without the index: read every heap page until 'Eleanor' is found.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: But notice — the index is a second place. Every time a row is inserted, updated, or deleted, the index must be updated too. If you have eight indexes on a table, every write pays eight times the cost. This is why "index everything" is a junior's mistake. Indexes trade write speed for read speed. Most production tables are read a hundred times per write — so the trade is usually worthwhile — but "usually" is not "always."

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And the engines disagree on storage. PostgreSQL keeps the heap and the indexes truly separate — every index, including the primary key, points into an unordered heap. MySQL's InnoDB stores the rows inside the primary-key B-tree itself; secondary indexes there hold the PK value and do a second lookup. SQL Server lets you choose. The differences matter when you reason about access cost — and when you read query plans, which we shall do shortly.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: One last lesson before we leave. PostgreSQL also supports partial indexes — an index that only covers rows matching a predicate. If your events ledger has a column archived that is true for ninety-five out of every hundred rows, an index on the active five percent is twenty times smaller and twenty times cheaper to maintain. Use them when one part of the data is hot and the rest is cold.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Reason about the structure

Before any retrieval check, study the layout below. Trace through these questions in your head:

  • If apprentices has 1,000,000 rows, roughly how many index-node reads does WHERE name = 'Eleanor' cost? (Hint: log of a million.)
  • If 8 indexes exist on the table, how many extra index updates does a single UPDATE apprentices SET xp = ... WHERE id = 42 cause? (Trick question — only the indexes covering xp need updating.)
  • The query WHERE archived = TRUE on a partial index WHERE archived = FALSE — can the index serve it?
  • In MySQL InnoDB, a secondary-index lookup costs how many B-tree traversals?
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- A B-tree index, conceptually:
--
--             [ K | M | T ]              <- root node (sorted keys)
--            /     |     \
--   [A..K]  [K..M] [M..T]  [T..Z]        <- internal nodes
--    leaves point into the heap.
--
-- Lookup of 'Eleanor': root says 'E' < 'K', go left.
-- Internal node refines further. Leaf returns (page, slot).
-- Total cost: depth of the tree (~3 for 1M rows).

CREATE INDEX idx_apprentices_name ON apprentices (name);

-- Partial index — only covers active rows:
CREATE INDEX idx_events_active_user
  ON events (user_id)
  WHERE archived = FALSE;

-- An equivalent secondary index in MySQL InnoDB stores the PK,
-- not a row pointer. So a lookup on (name) costs:
-- 1. Walk the (name) B-tree to find the PK value.
-- 2. Walk the (id) B-tree (which IS the table) to find the row.
-- Two B-tree traversals, not one.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior why an indexed lookup on a billion-row table only costs about 5 disk reads, while an unindexed lookup costs roughly the size of the entire table. Reference the B-tree's depth and the role of the heap.

questions.questionHtml: Why is a B-tree's lookup cost O(log N) instead of O(N)?
options: It is a balanced tree with high branching factor — every leaf is the same depth from the root, and that depth grows logarithmically with the number of keys
Because the leaves are stored in RAM
Because B-trees use compression
Because B-trees are written in assembly
questions.correctAnswer: It is a balanced tree with high branching factor — every leaf is the same depth from the root, and that depth grows logarithmically with the number of keys
questions.explanationHtml: The crucial properties are balance (every leaf is the same depth) and high branching factor (each node holds many keys, sized to fit a disk page). For 1M rows the depth is about 3; for 1B it is about 5. The lookup cost is the depth — a small constant for any practical table size. This is why indexed lookups don't get visibly slower as the table grows.

questions.questionHtml: Your workload is only equality lookups on a single column — no ranges, no ORDER BY, no prefix LIKE. The engine offers both B-tree and hash indexes. Which is the better choice and why?
options: Hash — equality lookups on hash are slightly faster (constant-time), and you don't need any of the ordering capabilities a B-tree provides
B-tree — hash indexes don't exist in SQL
B-tree — it is faster for equality than hash
Neither — use a full table scan
questions.correctAnswer: Hash — equality lookups on hash are slightly faster (constant-time), and you don't need any of the ordering capabilities a B-tree provides
questions.explanationHtml: Hash indexes are O(1) for equality versus B-tree's O(log N) — a small but real win on huge tables. The reason hash is rare is that it can't serve range queries, prefix LIKE, or ORDER BY because hashing destroys ordering. If your workload only needs equality, hash is better; B-tree is the universal default because it serves every pattern adequately. PostgreSQL supports both; MySQL InnoDB only B-tree (with an internal adaptive hash you can't directly create).

questions.questionHtml: An events table has 100,000,000 rows. 95% have archived = TRUE; only the 5% with archived = FALSE are queried frequently (always with a WHERE archived = FALSE AND user_id = ? filter). What's the most space- and write-efficient way to index for this workload in PostgreSQL?
options: A partial index: CREATE INDEX ON events (user_id) WHERE archived = FALSE — it covers only the 5% of rows that are queried, so it is 20× smaller and cheaper to maintain than a full index on user_id
A full B-tree on (user_id, archived) — composites are always best
No index at all — scans are fine on 100M rows
A hash index on archived
questions.correctAnswer: A partial index: CREATE INDEX ON events (user_id) WHERE archived = FALSE — it covers only the 5% of rows that are queried, so it is 20× smaller and cheaper to maintain than a full index on user_id
questions.explanationHtml: This is the canonical partial-index use case. The index contains only the rows you actually query, which means smaller on disk, fewer pages to read, and cheaper to maintain on inserts that don't touch the active partition. SQL Server calls these "filtered indexes"; MySQL has no equivalent. The query must include a matching WHERE archived = FALSE for the planner to use the partial index — that's how the planner proves the index is applicable.

questions.questionHtml: You're running MySQL with InnoDB. A query filters by a non-PK indexed column (WHERE email = ?) and selects all columns. Why does the engine perform two B-tree traversals instead of one?
options: InnoDB's clustered storage stores rows inside the primary-key B-tree. The secondary index on email holds the PK value, not a row pointer — so the engine walks the email index to get the PK, then walks the PK index to find the row
MySQL traverses every index for safety
It's a bug in InnoDB
All indexes in any engine require two traversals
questions.correctAnswer: InnoDB's clustered storage stores rows inside the primary-key B-tree. The secondary index on email holds the PK value, not a row pointer — so the engine walks the email index to get the PK, then walks the PK index to find the row
questions.explanationHtml: This is one of the most-tested differences between InnoDB and PostgreSQL in interviews. PostgreSQL's heap is unordered and every index — primary or secondary — points directly to a heap location, so a secondary lookup is one B-tree walk plus one heap fetch. InnoDB clusters the data inside the PK B-tree, so a secondary index stores the PK value and does a second B-tree walk to actually retrieve the row. SQL Server's clustered indexes behave the same way as InnoDB's when present.

subChunks.title: Selectivity & Composite Indexes — Building the Right Index
subChunks.hookHtml: Knowing what an index is is half the battle. The other half is knowing which index to add. Index the wrong column and the planner ignores it; index in the wrong order and the index serves only half the queries it could. The two ideas you'll use every day are selectivity and the leftmost-prefix rule.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
Selectivity — the fraction of rows a value matches

Selectivity is the ratio (distinct values / total rows), or equivalently "the fraction of rows the average filter value matches." High selectivity = filter narrows the result a lot. Low selectivity = the filter barely narrows anything.

ColumnDistinct / TotalSelectivityWorth indexing alone?
email (unique)1,000,000 / 1,000,0001.0Yes — points to one row
user_id in events50,000 / 1,000,0000.05Yes — average filter narrows to ~20 rows
status (5 values)5 / 1,000,0000.000005Maybe — depends on distribution
archived (boolean)2 / 1,000,0000.000002No — alone, useless

The folk-rule is: a B-tree pays off when the typical filter selects under ~5% of rows. Below that, the index lookup + heap fetch is cheaper than reading the heap sequentially. Above that, the engine often picks Seq Scan even when the index exists — many small random I/Os are slower than one big sequential read.

Distribution matters more than counts

Selectivity is an average. status has 5 values but if 95% of rows are status = 'OK' and 5% are 'WARN' / 'ERROR' / 'CRIT' / 'INFO', then a query for status = 'OK' is non-selective (95%) and a query for status = 'CRIT' is highly selective (~1%). Real engines maintain histograms per column — they know which values are frequent and which are rare, and they pick plans accordingly. This is why ANALYZE matters: stale histograms produce bad plans.

Composite indexes — order is everything

A composite index covers two or more columns in a fixed order:

CREATE INDEX idx_completions_app_quest_date
  ON completions (apprentice_id, quest_id, completed_at);

The index is sorted by apprentice_id first, then within each apprentice_id by quest_id, then within each pair by completed_at. The structure is exactly like a phone book sorted by surname, then forename, then address.

The leftmost-prefix rule

This is the rule every senior interviewer asks for. A composite index on (A, B, C) can serve queries that filter on:

  • A alone — yes, this is the leftmost prefix
  • A AND B — yes, leftmost two columns
  • A AND B AND C — yes, full prefix
  • A AND C — partially yes — the index helps with A but C-filtering is post-filter on the result
  • B alone — no — B is not a prefix of (A, B, C)
  • B AND C — no — same reason
  • C alone — no

Why? Because the index is sorted by A first. If you don't constrain A, the matching B-values for any given B are scattered across the entire index. The engine would have to scan every leaf to find them — not a seek but a full index scan, which is rarely faster than a heap scan.

Canonical column ordering for composites

The convention is (equality, equality, range, ORDER BY). Place the columns the query equates first, then the column that has a range filter, then any column you order by. Concretely:

-- Query: WHERE user_id = ? AND created_at BETWEEN ? AND ? ORDER BY created_at DESC
-- Best index: (user_id, created_at)
--   - user_id is an equality, goes first
--   - created_at is range AND order, goes second
-- This index serves the equality, the range, AND the ORDER BY without a sort step.

-- Query: WHERE user_id = ? AND status = 'ACTIVE'
-- Best index: (user_id, status) OR (status, user_id) — both equalities;
--   put the more selective column first.

Range and inequality columns kill the usefulness of any index columns to their right. Once the engine is doing a range scan on column 2, it cannot also seek on column 3 — it must filter column 3 row-by-row.

Covering indexes (index-only scans)

If an index contains every column a query reads, the engine never touches the heap — this is an index-only scan, the fastest possible plan. Composite indexes can be designed to cover specific queries:

-- Query: SELECT user_id, count FROM completions WHERE quest_id = 5;
-- Plain: CREATE INDEX ON completions (quest_id);
--   -> Index seek on quest_id, then heap fetch for (user_id, count)
-- Covering: CREATE INDEX ON completions (quest_id) INCLUDE (user_id, count);
--   -> Index-only scan, never touches the heap

PostgreSQL's INCLUDE clause adds non-key columns to leaves without making them part of the search key — the cleanest way to design covering indexes. SQL Server has the same INCLUDE. MySQL has no INCLUDE — you instead extend the key itself, which makes the index slightly larger but covering.

When NOT to index

  • Tiny tables. A 200-row table is faster to scan than to index-seek — random I/O loses to sequential I/O at small N.
  • Write-heavy bottlenecks. An audit log written 10,000×/sec but read once an hour does not need an index — every additional index slows every write.
  • Low-selectivity columns alone. An index on a boolean is rarely useful by itself; the planner will skip it.
  • Columns under a function. WHERE LOWER(name) = ? doesn't use an index on name. The fix is a functional index on LOWER(name), or storing already-normalised data.

storyBeats.text: Cipher pulls down a battered green ledger and lays it open. Each spread is a different column, each card-stack a different way of organising the same names.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Now you know what an index is. Today we ask the harder question: which index to build. The wrong index is worse than no index — it costs disk and writes and slows the planner, and the engine ignores it anyway. Two principles guide everything: selectivity, and the leftmost-prefix rule.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Selectivity is the fraction of rows a typical filter value matches. email is highly selective — every row is unique, so a filter picks one row in a million. archived, a boolean where ninety-five percent of rows are TRUE, is dreadfully unselective — the filter picks nine hundred and fifty thousand rows out of a million. The first is worth indexing. The second, alone, is not. The folk-rule: index columns where typical filter values match under five percent of rows.

storyBeats.speaker: The leftmost-prefix rule
storyBeats.text:
-- Composite index, columns ordered (apprentice_id, quest_id, completed_at):
CREATE INDEX idx_completions_app_quest_date
  ON completions (apprentice_id, quest_id, completed_at);

-- Queries this index serves:
WHERE apprentice_id = 1                                  -- yes (prefix: A)
WHERE apprentice_id = 1 AND quest_id = 2                 -- yes (prefix: A,B)
WHERE apprentice_id = 1 AND quest_id = 2
  AND completed_at > '2026-01-01'                        -- yes (full prefix)

-- Queries this index does NOT serve:
WHERE quest_id = 2                                       -- NO (not a prefix)
WHERE completed_at > '2026-01-01'                        -- NO
WHERE quest_id = 2 AND completed_at > '2026-01-01'       -- NO

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Picture a phone book sorted by surname, then forename, then address. You can look up everyone called 'Eleanor Smith' — surname narrows you to a chapter, forename narrows you to a page. But you cannot use it to look up 'everyone whose forename is Eleanor', because the Eleanors are scattered across every surname-chapter. That is the leftmost-prefix rule, exactly.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: The canonical column order is equality, then range, then sort. Equality columns first because they prune the tree most effectively. The range column next because once you start scanning a range, the columns to its right are no longer useful for seeking — only for post-filtering. Get this order wrong and the index is half-blind.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And the prize at the top: a covering index. If the index leaves contain every column the query reads, the engine never touches the heap at all. Postgres calls this an index-only scan, the fastest plan there is. Use CREATE INDEX ... INCLUDE (...) to attach extra columns to the leaves without making them part of the search key. The discipline: design indexes for your hot queries, not for individual columns.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Last warning. WHERE LOWER(name) = 'eleanor' does not use an index on name. The index is sorted by name, but you are asking about a computed value. The fix is either a functional index — CREATE INDEX ON apprentices (LOWER(name)) — or store the data already lowercased and avoid the function on the lookup. The same trap fires for any function applied to an indexed column. Recognise it, name it, fix it.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Pick the right index for each workload

For each query pattern below, decide what index would best serve it. Walk through it in your head before checking against the answers. The composite index in the schema is idx_completions_app_quest_date ON completions(apprentice_id, quest_id, completed_at).
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- Existing index on completions:
-- idx_completions_app_quest_date (apprentice_id, quest_id, completed_at)

-- ====================================================================
-- Workload 1:
SELECT * FROM completions WHERE apprentice_id = 1;
-- USES the index. apprentice_id is the leftmost prefix.

-- Workload 2:
SELECT * FROM completions WHERE apprentice_id = 1 AND quest_id = 5;
-- USES the index. Two-column prefix.

-- Workload 3:
SELECT * FROM completions WHERE quest_id = 5;
-- DOES NOT use the index — quest_id alone is not a prefix.
-- Add: CREATE INDEX ON completions (quest_id);

-- Workload 4:
SELECT * FROM completions
WHERE apprentice_id = 1 AND completed_at > '2026-01-01';
-- USES the index for apprentice_id, then post-filters completed_at.
-- Could be improved by an index (apprentice_id, completed_at)
-- if quest_id is rarely filtered.

-- ====================================================================
-- Workload 5: a covering candidate
SELECT apprentice_id, quest_id
FROM completions
WHERE apprentice_id = 1;
-- Index-only scan! All projected columns are in the index leaves.

-- ====================================================================
-- Workload 6: function on indexed column
SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE LOWER(name) = 'eleanor';
-- DOES NOT use idx_apprentices_name. Fix with a functional index:
CREATE INDEX ON apprentices (LOWER(name));

-- ====================================================================
-- Workload 7: low-selectivity boolean
SELECT * FROM events WHERE archived = TRUE;
-- Even with an index on archived, the planner likely picks Seq Scan
-- because the filter matches ~95% of rows. The index doesn't pay.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Explain to a junior why a composite index on (user_id, created_at) serves WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC with no sort step required, but cannot serve WHERE created_at > ? alone. Use the phone-book analogy.

questions.questionHtml: What does selectivity mean for an indexed column?
options: The fraction of rows a typical filter value matches — high selectivity means each value is rare and the index narrows the result aggressively
The size of the index in bytes
The cost of inserting a new row
How quickly the index was created
questions.correctAnswer: The fraction of rows a typical filter value matches — high selectivity means each value is rare and the index narrows the result aggressively
questions.explanationHtml: Selectivity ≈ distinct_values / total_rows. A unique-email column has selectivity 1.0 (each value picks one row). A boolean column has selectivity 2/N (each value picks roughly half). High selectivity = good index candidate. The folk-rule: index pays off when the typical filter selects under ~5% of rows.

questions.questionHtml: You have a composite index idx ON orders (customer_id, status, created_at). Which query cannot use this index?
options: WHERE status = 'SHIPPED' — status is the second column, not a prefix; the engine has no way to seek into the index without first knowing customer_id
WHERE customer_id = 7
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'SHIPPED'
WHERE customer_id = 7 AND status = 'SHIPPED' AND created_at > '2026-01-01'
questions.correctAnswer: WHERE status = 'SHIPPED' — status is the second column, not a prefix; the engine has no way to seek into the index without first knowing customer_id
questions.explanationHtml: The leftmost-prefix rule. The index is sorted by customer_id first; without constraining customer_id, the matching status values are scattered across the entire index. The other three queries all begin with customer_id and can use it. Phone-book analogy: you can find 'Smith, Eleanor' but not 'every Eleanor' in a book sorted surname-first.

questions.questionHtml: Your hottest query is SELECT created_at, total FROM orders WHERE user_id = ? ORDER BY created_at DESC. Which index gives the best plan?
options: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (total) — equality column first, ORDER BY column next (so no sort step), and INCLUDE makes it a covering index for an index-only scan
CREATE INDEX ON orders (created_at, user_id) — date first since ORDER BY uses it
CREATE INDEX ON orders (total)
No index — the planner will figure it out
questions.correctAnswer: CREATE INDEX ON orders (user_id, created_at) INCLUDE (total) — equality column first, ORDER BY column next (so no sort step), and INCLUDE makes it a covering index for an index-only scan
questions.explanationHtml: This applies all three rules: (1) equality column (user_id) leftmost, (2) the ORDER BY column (created_at) next so the index walk is already sorted and no Sort step is needed, (3) INCLUDE (total) attaches the projected non-key column to the leaves, enabling an index-only scan that never touches the heap. Putting created_at first would let the engine read in date order but it'd have to scan the whole index to find user_id matches.

questions.questionHtml: A junior wants to add an index on archived (a boolean column where ~95% of rows have archived = TRUE) to speed up WHERE archived = FALSE AND user_id = ?. What's the best advice?
options: Add a partial index: CREATE INDEX ON events (user_id) WHERE archived = FALSE. The index covers only the 5% of rows that match the predicate, so it is small, cheap to maintain, and serves the query directly
Add a plain index on archived — it will solve the problem
Add separate indexes on archived and user_id, the planner will combine them
Don't index — booleans cannot be indexed
questions.correctAnswer: Add a partial index: CREATE INDEX ON events (user_id) WHERE archived = FALSE. The index covers only the 5% of rows that match the predicate, so it is small, cheap to maintain, and serves the query directly
questions.explanationHtml: A plain index on archived alone is useless — selectivity is 2/N, and the planner will scan instead. Indexing (archived, user_id) works but is mostly wasted space (95% of the index is the unused TRUE branch). The partial index keys on user_id but only stores the 5% of rows where the predicate is satisfied. Smaller, faster, cheaper to maintain. SQL Server calls these "filtered indexes"; MySQL has no equivalent.

subChunks.title: EXPLAIN — Reading the Engine's Mind
subChunks.hookHtml: Before you tune a query, you have to see what the engine is actually doing. EXPLAIN shows the query plan — the tree of operations the engine will execute. Reading a plan is one of the highest-leverage skills in database engineering: a 30-second EXPLAIN can find a missing index that would have taken hours of trial-and-error to debug.
subChunks.explanationHtml:
EXPLAIN vs EXPLAIN ANALYZE

CommandWhat it doesSafe on writes?
EXPLAINShows the planner's chosen plan and estimated costs and row counts. Does not run the query.Yes — pure planning
EXPLAIN ANALYZERuns the query and shows estimate and actual row counts and timings.NO on UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT — those modifications happen for real. Wrap in BEGIN; ROLLBACK; if you only want the plan.
EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS)PostgreSQL extension — also shows shared/local buffer hits and reads. Essential for diagnosing I/O-bound queries.Same as ANALYZE

Use EXPLAIN when you want to know what the planner thinks. Use EXPLAIN ANALYZE when you want to know what actually happens. The gap between the two is where most performance bugs live.

The plan tree — read bottom-up

Every plan is a tree. Each node is an operator. Children produce rows; parents consume and transform them. The root produces the final result. Read it bottom-up — leaves are scans, intermediate nodes are joins/sorts/aggregates, the root is the output.

EXPLAIN
SELECT a.name, q.title
FROM apprentices a
JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
JOIN quests      q ON q.id = c.quest_id
WHERE a.rank = 'Mage';
Hash Join  (cost=2.20..18.40 rows=8 width=64)
  Hash Cond: (q.id = c.quest_id)
  ->  Seq Scan on quests q  (cost=0.00..14.50 rows=300 width=36)
  ->  Hash  (cost=2.10..2.10 rows=8 width=36)
        ->  Hash Join  (cost=1.05..2.10 rows=8 width=36)
              Hash Cond: (c.apprentice_id = a.id)
              ->  Seq Scan on completions c  (cost=0.00..1.06 rows=8 width=12)
              ->  Hash  (cost=1.04..1.04 rows=2 width=32)
                    ->  Index Scan using idx_apprentices_rank on apprentices a
                          (cost=0.00..1.04 rows=2 width=32)
                          Index Cond: (rank = 'Mage')

Reading: index-scan apprentices for rank='Mage' (2 rows). Hash those. Seq-scan completions, hash-join against the apprentice hash. Hash-join the result against quests by quest_id. Two-step hash join, anchored on a tiny indexed seek.

Decoding the cost numbers

PostgreSQL's cost=startup..total rows=N width=W:

  • startup — the cost paid before the first row is returned (e.g. building a hash, reading the first index page)
  • total — the cost paid by the time the last row is returned
  • rows — the planner's estimate of how many rows this operator emits
  • width — average row size in bytes

The cost units are arbitrary planner-units, not seconds. They're useful for relative comparison between plans, not as absolute predictions. EXPLAIN ANALYZE adds actual time=startup..total rows=N loops=L — the real numbers.

The access methods you'll see most

OperatorWhat it doesWhen it appears
Seq ScanReads every row of the table sequentiallyNo usable index, or the table is small enough that scanning is faster than seeking
Index ScanWalks the index, then fetches matching rows from the heapIndex covers WHERE filter, selectivity is high enough
Index Only ScanWalks the index alone — never fetches from the heapThe index is covering for this query (every projected column is in the index)
Bitmap Heap ScanBuilds a bitmap of matching row IDs from one or more indexes, then fetches the heap pages in bulkMid-selectivity filters where pure index scan would do many random fetches
Nested LoopFor each row of the outer side, look up matching rows on the inner side (often via index)Small outer side, indexed inner side
Hash JoinBuild a hash table from one side, probe with the otherMedium-sized inputs without sort order; equi-joins only
Merge JoinSort both sides, walk in parallelBoth inputs already sorted (e.g. by index), or large inputs where sorting is worth it

The classic gotcha — estimated vs actual

EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
--   Index Scan using idx_orders_user (cost=...) (actual rows=1000000 loops=1)
--     Index Cond: (user_id = 42)
--   Planning Time: 0.4 ms
--   Execution Time: 4500 ms
-- Estimated rows = 8, actual rows = 1,000,000.

The planner estimated 8 rows for this user but found a million. That's a 5-orders-of-magnitude error and almost certainly causes a bad join algorithm choice if this query joins to anything else. The fix is ANALYZE orders; — run the table's statistics collector. PostgreSQL has autovacuum/autoanalyze that runs in the background, but heavy bulk loads can outpace it.

The N+1 trap — how it surfaces in EXPLAIN

An ORM that fetches one parent then one query per child produces an application-side N+1, invisible to the database. But sometimes a SQL query has the same shape internally. In the plan you'll see a Nested Loop with a high loops count and the same Index Scan on the inner side:

Nested Loop  (cost=... rows=10 width=...) (actual time=... loops=10000)
  ->  Seq Scan on orders     -- 10,000 rows out
  ->  Index Scan on order_items  -- runs 10,000 TIMES — once per outer row

Each loop is cheap on its own — an indexed lookup — but ten thousand of them add up. The fix is usually a Hash Join (build the hash once, probe N times) or a JOIN restructure, plus possibly a covering index. SET enable_nestloop = OFF; can force a different plan to confirm.

When the planner picks Seq Scan over Index Scan

It's not always wrong! Reasons the planner legitimately picks Seq Scan even when an index exists:

  1. Low selectivity. If 50% of rows match the filter, doing 50% of the table as random index lookups is slower than one sequential scan. Random I/O is dramatically slower than sequential I/O.
  2. Small table. Under a few thousand rows, scanning the heap is in microseconds. The index seek isn't worth it.
  3. Stale statistics. The planner thinks the filter is non-selective when it actually is. ANALYZE fixes it.
  4. Function on indexed column. WHERE LOWER(name) = ? can't use an index on name — the planner falls back to scan.
  5. Type mismatch. WHERE id = '42' against an integer column may force an implicit cast that defeats the index. Match the literal type to the column.

The seven questions to ask any plan

  1. Are we scanning when we should be seeking? (Seq Scan + small selective filter = missing index.)
  2. Are estimated and actual row counts close? (Big mismatches = stale stats; run ANALYZE.)
  3. Is the join order surprising? (Tiny table joined first is usually right; massive table first is usually a stats issue.)
  4. Is there a Sort step that an index could eliminate?
  5. Is a Nested Loop running thousands of inner-side iterations? (Likely an N+1-shaped plan.)
  6. What's the most expensive node? (Look at actual time; 80% of query time is usually in one operation.)
  7. Are we returning more rows than we use upstream? (Excess rows that get filtered later are wasted I/O.)

storyBeats.text: Cipher pulls a peculiar lens from a drawer — a thin glass disc set in a brass frame. He hands it to you, holding it up to the lantern so you can see the etched runes around the rim.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: When a query is slow, do not guess. Look. EXPLAIN is the lens that lets you see what the engine plans to do. Every database has it. Every senior database hand reads it. The plan is a tree of operators — leaves are scans, branches are joins and sorts and aggregates, the root is the result. Read bottom-up.

storyBeats.speaker: Reading a Postgres plan
storyBeats.text:
EXPLAIN
SELECT a.name FROM apprentices a
JOIN completions c ON c.apprentice_id = a.id
WHERE a.rank = 'Mage';

-- Hash Join                            (cost=4..50 rows=10 width=32)
--   Hash Cond: (c.apprentice_id = a.id)
--   ->  Seq Scan on completions c      (cost=0..30 rows=100 width=8)
--   ->  Hash                           (cost=4..4 rows=2 width=32)
--         ->  Index Scan using idx_apprentices_rank on apprentices a
--               (cost=0..4 rows=2 width=32)
--               Index Cond: (rank = 'Mage')

-- Reading bottom-up:
-- 1. Index-scan apprentices for rank='Mage'. 2 rows.
-- 2. Hash those 2 rows.
-- 3. Seq-scan completions (no usable index on apprentice_id alone).
-- 4. Hash-join probes each completion against the hash. ~10 matches.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Three access methods dominate every plan. Seq Scan reads every row of a table — fine on small tables, ruinous on large ones with selective filters. Index Scan walks the index then fetches matching heap rows. Index Only Scan is the prize — the engine answers the entire query from the index alone, never touching the heap. The three join algorithms — Nested Loop, Hash Join, Merge Join — are picked by the optimiser, not by you. Knowing what they mean lets you spot when a join is the bottleneck.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: And use EXPLAIN ANALYZE for tuning. Plain EXPLAIN shows the planner's estimate. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and shows the actual row counts and times. Big gaps between estimate and actual usually mean the table's statistics are stale — run ANALYZE tablename; to refresh them. The single most common reason for a sudden query slowdown in production is exactly this: stale stats, the optimiser picks a bad plan, latency triples overnight, three engineers spend a morning debugging.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: Warning: EXPLAIN ANALYZE on UPDATE or DELETE actually performs the modification. Wrap it in BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK; if you only want to see the plan. I have seen apprentices accidentally delete a thousand production rows because they forgot. The lens cuts both ways.

storyBeats.speaker: Cipher the Archivist
storyBeats.text: When you read a plan, ask seven questions. Are we scanning when we should be seeking? Are the estimated rows close to the actual rows? Is the join order surprising? Is there a Sort step an index could eliminate? Is a Nested Loop running thousands of iterations on the inner side — the N+1 trap? What is the single most expensive operator? Are we emitting more rows than we will keep? Walk that checklist down any plan and you will find the bottleneck nine times in ten.

subChunks.guidedPracticeHtml:
📜 Diagnose each plan

Read each EXPLAIN fragment below. For each, identify what the engine is doing and whether anything looks wrong. The plans use Postgres syntax — the most common dialect.
subChunks.guidedPracticeStarterCode:
-- ====================================================================
-- Plan A — fast lookup with the implicit PK index
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE id = 1;
-- Index Scan using apprentices_pkey  (cost=0.28..8.30 rows=1 width=64)
--   Index Cond: (id = 1)
--
-- READ: PK is auto-indexed; this is a single-row index seek. Optimal.

-- ====================================================================
-- Plan B — full scan, suspect missing index
EXPLAIN SELECT * FROM apprentices WHERE rank = 'Mage';
-- Seq Scan on apprentices  (cost=0.00..1700 rows=4 width=64)
--   Filter: (rank = 'Mage')
--
-- READ: 4 rows out of millions, but the engine reads them all to find them.
-- FIX:  CREATE INDEX idx_apprentices_rank ON apprentices(rank);
--       BUT only if rank is selective. If 95% of rows are Mage, the index
--       will not pay; the planner will keep choosing Seq Scan.

-- ====================================================================
-- Plan C — sort step that an index could eliminate
EXPLAIN
SELECT * FROM apprentices ORDER BY name LIMIT 10;
-- Limit  (cost=18.50..18.53 rows=10 width=64)
--   ->  Sort  (cost=18.50..23.00 rows=1800 width=64)         <- expensive
--         Sort Key: name
--         ->  Seq Scan on apprentices
--
-- READ: every row must be sorted before the LIMIT can apply.
-- FIX:  CREATE INDEX idx_apprentices_name ON apprentices(name);
--       Plan becomes Index Scan that walks first 10 names directly. No Sort.

-- ====================================================================
-- Plan D — N+1-shaped Nested Loop
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT o.id, oi.product_id
FROM orders o
JOIN order_items oi ON oi.order_id = o.id;
-- Nested Loop  (cost=...) (actual time=... rows=50000 loops=1)
--   ->  Seq Scan on orders          (actual rows=10000 loops=1)
--   ->  Index Scan on order_items   (actual rows=5 loops=10000)
--                                              ^^^^^^^^^^
-- READ: the inner Index Scan ran 10,000 times — once per outer row.
--       Total: 10,000 random index seeks.
-- FIX:  hint or restructure to a Hash Join: build hash on order_items.order_id
--       once, probe with each order. SET enable_nestloop=off; to force.

-- ====================================================================
-- Plan E — estimate vs actual diverges
EXPLAIN ANALYZE
SELECT * FROM orders WHERE user_id = 42;
-- Index Scan using idx_orders_user (cost=... rows=8) (actual rows=1000000)
--   Index Cond: (user_id = 42)
-- Planning Time: 0.4 ms  Execution Time: 4500 ms
--
-- READ: planner expected 8 rows, found 1,000,000. 5-order-of-magnitude
--       estimation error usually causes a bad join algorithm downstream.
-- FIX:  ANALYZE orders;  -- refresh the table's statistics.
subChunks.feynmanPrompt: Walk a junior through reading an EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan. Use Plan E above as your example: explain why a 5-order-of-magnitude gap between estimated and actual rows is dangerous, what causes it, and the one-command fix.

questions.questionHtml: What is the difference between EXPLAIN and EXPLAIN ANALYZE?
options: EXPLAIN shows the planner's estimate without running the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports both the estimate and the real row counts and timings
They are aliases — same output
EXPLAIN ANALYZE only works on SELECT, EXPLAIN only works on UPDATE
EXPLAIN requires a license
questions.correctAnswer: EXPLAIN shows the planner's estimate without running the query. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually runs the query and reports both the estimate and the real row counts and timings
questions.explanationHtml: Plain EXPLAIN is planning only — safe on any statement. EXPLAIN ANALYZE actually executes the query, which means it is destructive on UPDATE/DELETE/INSERT. Wrap those in BEGIN; EXPLAIN ANALYZE ...; ROLLBACK; if you only want to see the plan. PostgreSQL adds (BUFFERS) for I/O details; MySQL has its own EXPLAIN ANALYZE with similar semantics.

questions.questionHtml: Your EXPLAIN ANALYZE shows rows=8 estimated but actual rows=1,000,000. What's the single most likely cause and the standard fix?
options: Stale statistics — the planner's histograms haven't been refreshed since a recent bulk load. Run ANALYZE tablename; to update them, then re-EXPLAIN
EXPLAIN is broken in this Postgres version
The query is incorrect SQL
Estimates are always wrong; ignore them
questions.correctAnswer: Stale statistics — the planner's histograms haven't been refreshed since a recent bulk load. Run ANALYZE tablename; to update them, then re-EXPLAIN
questions.explanationHtml: The optimiser uses statistics (row counts, value distributions, NDVs) to choose access methods and join algorithms. When stats are stale — typically after a big bulk insert/delete or right after a schema migration — estimates can be orders of magnitude off, leading to bad plans (e.g. picking a Nested Loop when a Hash Join would be 100× faster). PostgreSQL's autovacuum auto-analyses, but heavy bulk loads can outpace it. Run ANALYZE tablename; manually after bulk operations.

questions.questionHtml: Two queries on the same table show very different speeds. Their plans show the slow one uses Seq Scan and the fast one uses Index Scan. Both filter on the same indexed column. What's the most likely difference?
options: The slow query applies a function or implicit cast to the indexed column (e.g. WHERE LOWER(name) = ? or WHERE id = '42' against an integer column). The function/cast computes a different value per row, so the index cannot be used to seek
The slow query is missing a WHERE clause
Index Scan is always faster than Seq Scan; the slow one must have a bug
The slow query uses a different storage engine internally
questions.correctAnswer: The slow query applies a function or implicit cast to the indexed column (e.g. WHERE LOWER(name) = ? or WHERE id = '42' against an integer column). The function/cast computes a different value per row, so the index cannot be used to seek
questions.explanationHtml: The canonical "my index isn't being used" gotcha. WHERE LOWER(name) = ? can't use an index on name because the engine would have to compute LOWER for every row to find matches. Same trap fires for implicit type casts: WHERE id = '42' against an INT column may insert a cast that defeats the index. Fixes: functional indexes (CREATE INDEX ON apprentices (LOWER(name))), normalising data on insert, or matching literal types to column types. Note: "Index Scan is always faster than Seq Scan" is FALSE — for non-selective filters, Seq Scan can be faster because it reads sequentially while Index Scan does many random heap fetches.

questions.questionHtml: An EXPLAIN ANALYZE plan shows a Nested Loop whose inner Index Scan reports actual rows=5 loops=10000. The query takes 4 seconds. What is the most likely problem and a reasonable next step?
options: The plan is N+1-shaped — the inner index lookup ran 10,000 times. Each lookup is cheap, but 10,000 random seeks add up. Investigate forcing a Hash Join (build the lookup table once, probe N times) and check whether refreshing statistics would change the planner's choice
Indexes are corrupt — rebuild them
The query is fine; 4 seconds is normal for any join
Drop all indexes and re-run
questions.correctAnswer: The plan is N+1-shaped — the inner index lookup ran 10,000 times. Each lookup is cheap, but 10,000 random seeks add up. Investigate forcing a Hash Join (build the lookup table once, probe N times) and check whether refreshing statistics would change the planner's choice
questions.explanationHtml: The loops=10000 on an inner Index Scan is the N+1 signature inside the database. The total work is per-loop time × loops — even microsecond seeks become seconds at that scale. The fix is usually a Hash Join (build the hash on the smaller side once, probe with the larger side) which the planner picks when stats are accurate. SET enable_nestloop = OFF; at the session level forces the planner to consider alternatives — useful for confirming the diagnosis. Long term: refresh stats with ANALYZE, and consider whether the join can be restructured (e.g. denormalising or aggregating differently).
